title: Who Pays for What We Know
gist: Grace Werner argues that AI labs and their founders (OpenAI Foundation, Anthropic cofounders) are becoming the dominant funders of research on AI's own consequences, echoing Rockefeller-era 'scientific philanthropy'. The core risk is not capture but 'institutional dependence': funders set the research agenda while public epistemic capacity (GAO, CRS, OTA) has eroded, so the questions that go unfunded matter most.

insights.claim: Grace Werner argues AI tycoons' power exceeds Rockefeller's because it is over information itself: as decision-makers delegate thinking to AI systems, even seemingly independent organizations may produce their output and views via the labs' models.
insights.speaker: Grace Werner
insights.so_what: AI labs' influence over policy discourse may compound through both funding and model usage, raising regulatory and reputational stakes.

insights.claim: Drawing on Michael Polanyi's 'republic of science', Grace Werner argues that formal freedom to publish unwelcome conclusions differs from practical capacity to pursue questions outside established funding priorities.
insights.speaker: Grace Werner
insights.so_what: Independence of AI research should be judged by funding diversity, not publication freedom.

insights.claim: Grace Werner notes that elected policymakers mostly act on problems already measured, modeled and translated into proposals, so questions lacking funded methods or advocates may never enter political consideration — giving research funders agenda-setting power over AI regulation.
insights.speaker: Grace Werner
insights.so_what: Whoever funds AI-impact measurement effectively shapes which AI regulations get proposed.

insights.claim: Between 1979 and 2015 the Government Accountability Office staff shrank 44%, the Congressional Research Service 28% and congressional committee staff 38%, and Congress eliminated the Office of Technology Assessment in 1995.
insights.speaker: Grace Werner
insights.so_what: Congress lacks in-house technical capacity to understand AI, increasing reliance on lab-funded and lobbyist expertise.
insights.locator: That public capacity has since eroded.

insights.claim: Political scientists Timothy LaPira and Herschel Thomas found that more than half of registered federal lobbyists are former government officials, filling a congressional expertise vacuum.
insights.speaker: Grace Werner
insights.so_what: Lobbying-driven expertise means well-funded industries (like AI) disproportionately shape legislation.
insights.locator: That public capacity has since eroded.

insights.claim: Grace Werner argues government dependence on outside expertise is self-reinforcing: the more expertise outside institutions supply, the less government pays for internally, and outside bodies outbid government for scarce specialists.
insights.speaker: Grace Werner
insights.so_what: Absent new public institutions (an OTA-style body), AI policy will be increasingly shaped by industry-funded experts.
insights.quote: Dependence, once established, tends to deepen.

insights.claim: Grace Werner argues economic transformation shifts the distribution of epistemic capacity faster than political institutions can adapt, and that Progressive Era institutions like the Bureau of Labor Statistics and Federal Trade Commission were the historical counterweight to industrialist-funded knowledge.
insights.speaker: Grace Werner
insights.so_what: Watch for proposals to build public AI-measurement capacity as a potential regulatory inflection.
